_README: The fixture corpus, as a manifest rather than copies.
Each entry names one filing, why it earns a place, and a measured claim that
test_fixtures.py asserts. If a claim stops holding, the pathology moved and every
ticket reasoning from it needs rechecking - that is the point of verifying them.
WHY A MANIFEST AND NOT COPIED FILES:
1. Truncating is unsafe. ingest.py's _LATE_DETECTION guard is a *fraction* of body
length (0.9), so shortening a file changes whether header detection counts as
'late' - a truncated fixture can segment differently from the real filing and
2. Copying whole files means ~6.4 MB of duplicated public-domain text that is
already on disk, in a repo where edgar_corpus/ is gitignored precisely because
the brief links it for redownload.
3. The suite already requires the corpus. 21 of the 64 free-tier tests read it, and
test_smoke.py::test_corpus_is_present asserts it. A manifest matches how the
suite already works instead of inventing a second source of truth.

fixtures.why: Largest inline-XBRL residue in the corpus - 86,721 tokens on a single line (§2.3). At 800 tokens/chunk this alone would emit ~108 chunks of pure tag soup.
ALL-CAPS item headers, form C (§2.5). Tesla is also the §2.4 exemplar for a whole Item 1A on one line.

Item headers glued behind page furniture, form B (§2.5). Also one of the 54 filings with NO 'Report Period' header, so it exercises the fiscal-year fallback - and it is an off-calendar (September) filer.

Zero-space item headers COMBINED with ALL CAPS - 'ITEM 6.E' (§2.5 forms C and D at once, which is harder than either alone). Measured: the arch doc's zero-space example is from a 10-Q, not the 10-K - GOOG's 10-K writes 'Item 9A.' with normal spacing, so picking the 10-K tests nothing. Corpus ticker is GOOG, not GOOGL.

Second zero-space filer and an independent check that form D is not a Google-only quirk - Meta writes it mixed-case ('Item 9A.C') where GOOG writes it in caps, so the two fixtures cover both casings of the same defect.

Pipe item headers, forms A and A-prime, where the trailing page number is the only discriminator between a TOC row and a real header (§2.5). ALSO the clearest fiscal_year off-by-one: labelled FY2026, covers FY2025.
Largest filing in the corpus and the most table-dense, so it is the worst case for table-caption binding (§2.7). Also the thin side of the quota asymmetry - 4 filings against Apple's 16 (§2.9).
The 10-K baseline for the panel's temporal question. Ticket 08 must guarantee this is in context rather than answering from 10-Q amendments alone.

The off-calendar 10-Q whose metadata contradicts its own text: period_end 2025-10-26 yields fiscal_year 2025, while the filing says 'fiscal year 2026' 53 times. This is citation [C11] in ticket 01's NVIDIA run, rendered as FY2025 above an excerpt about fiscal 2026. Also a 10-Q Item 1A material-changes case (§4.4).
Its sole bare-regex item match is an 'Item 601(a)' Reg S-K citation - a phantom header (§2.5). Any segmenter that treats it as a real header mis-segments the whole filing.
The ONLY filing with no cover-page anchor at all, even case-insensitively. This is the file that forces ticket 03's fallback (§2.3 suggests cutting at the first FORM 10-[KQ]).

The second of §2.3's '244/246' anchor misses - but it misses only because the arch doc's regex is case-SENSITIVE. Adding re.IGNORECASE recovers it for free, so ticket 03 needs a fallback for one file, not two. Kept as a fixture so that stays true.
Second fiscal_year off-by-one, on a different year boundary from AMZN: labelled 2025, covers 2024. Two independent cases stop ticket 15's fix being tuned to one filing.
